subject_options: Should a competing venue stay in your Google Ads?
Your team knows something your search terms don't
What a competing venue search can't tell us
email.preview: The report shows the name. Your team knows whether couples actually compare you.

email.body:
Hi {{contact.first_name}},

Carmen, our Google Ads lead, was going through a venue client's search terms with a member of their team recently, and another venue's name came up.

Carmen's usual starting point with competitor searches is to leave them in. The team member explained that some couples had considered that venue before considering theirs.

So there was a reason to give that search some consideration.

A little later in the review, a different venue came up. This time the team member explained that it served a different market. "That's nowhere near," she said. Couples choosing that venue weren't weighing it against theirs, and Carmen agreed that one should be excluded.

So there were two venue names in the same report and two different recommendations. What separated them came from the venue's team, not from the account.

**A venue name in your search terms can't tell us whether those couples would ever consider yours.**

Honestly? Your team may already know the answer. You hear it on tours and inquiry calls, in the places couples mention and the ones that never come up.

That's why we want the account data and your knowledge of local couples in the same conversation. We bring the advertising judgment. You bring what you know about the couples who actually compare you.

If you run your own Google Ads and want an expert working through those decisions with you, our Google Search Accelerator is built for exactly that: we build and launch your campaigns, and you run them with our experts beside you.

If there's a Google Ads decision you'd like expert support with, reply to this email and tell me a bit about what you're trying to solve.

Talk soon,
Whitney

reels.script:
Our Google Ads lead, Carmen, was going through a venue client's search terms with someone from their team, and another venue's name popped up.

Now, Carmen's default with competitor searches is to leave them in. In her words, "my default is always just leave competitors in."

And the team member explained that some couples had considered that venue before considering theirs.

Then a little later, a different venue came up. And this time she said, "That's nowhere near." Different market. Those couples weren't comparing the two venues. So Carmen agreed that one should be excluded.

Same report, two venue names, two different calls. And the thing that made the difference wasn't anywhere in the account. It was what the venue's team hears from couples.

That's why we want the account data and your knowledge of local couples in the same conversation. A name in a search report tells us what someone typed. It doesn't tell us whether those couples would ever consider your venue. Your team might already know that part, and we want to hear it before we make a recommendation.
reels.caption:
Your team hears which other venues couples are weighing. A search report doesn't.

When you run your own Google Ads, competitor names show up in your search terms a lot. Some look like an obvious cut. Some look worth keeping. And it's fair to wonder whether the person advising you knows which is which for your venue and your couples.

In a recent review, Carmen, our Google Ads lead, went through those searches with a member of a venue client's team. The team knew couples had considered one nearby venue as well as theirs. Another, the team explained, was in a different market entirely. Carmen agreed that one should be excluded.

The venue names alone wouldn't have sorted those two. The team's knowledge of their couples did.

That's how we want competitor decisions to work: the account data and what you know about local couples on the table together, with us responsible for the recommendation we make.

-Whitney

reels.on_screen_hook: I don't think a competing venue's name should decide your Google Ads on its own.
reels.script:
I don't think a competing venue's name should decide on its own whether a Google Ads search stays or goes.

Here's what I mean. When another venue shows up in your search terms, the account can tell us someone typed that name. What it can't tell us is whether those couples would ever look at your venue too. And honestly, the people who usually know that are you and your team. You hear it on tours. You hear it on inquiry calls.

We saw this in a recent review. One nearby venue, the client's team knew couples had considered alongside theirs. Another, they told Carmen, our Google Ads lead, was a different market entirely, and she agreed that one should be excluded.

So that's how we want to work with venues. We bring the advertising judgment. But we want your knowledge of local couples in the conversation before we make a recommendation, because that's what tells us which comparisons are real.
reels.caption:
Some of the most useful information for your Google Ads lives in your inquiry calls.

If you run your own campaigns, you've probably looked at a list of search terms and seen other venues' names. You might keep them all, cut them all, or go with your gut. Meanwhile, your team knows which places couples bring up on tours and which ones never come up at all.

We think those two things should meet. In a review with one of our venue clients, the team explained that couples had considered one nearby venue as well as theirs. A second venue served a different market, and Carmen, our Google Ads lead, agreed with excluding it.

We bring the advertising judgment. We just want our recommendations built on what your couples actually compare, so the searches you keep are the ones that make sense for your venue.

-Whitney

reels.caption:
A venue can look like your competitor on paper and never be on your couples' shortlist.

And the reverse is true too. Couples planning a wedding don't always compare the places you'd expect, and your team is often the first to hear about it, whether that's on a tour, an inquiry call or a quick question at the end of a consultation.

In a recent review, Carmen, our Google Ads lead, went through a venue client's search terms with a member of their team. The team knew couples had looked at one nearby venue too, so that search had a real reason to be there. Another venue came up, and the team explained it was nowhere near their market. Carmen agreed it should be excluded.

We believe good Google Ads guidance hears that context before it recommends anything. The report brings the names forward. The people who talk to couples explain which ones matter.

-Whitney

You can know your local couples better than anyone and still want a specialist beside you when a Google Ads decision comes up.

Couples had considered one nearby venue alongside theirs. A second served a market the team didn't see overlapping with their own, and Carmen agreed with excluding it.

before_publishing: Get recorded client permission for this anonymous exchange, the comparisons couples reported and the quoted lines (including Erin's "That's nowhere near."). Hold every asset until permission is recorded.
Confirm that Erin can accurately be described as a member of the client's team. Don't call her the owner or give her a role.

Keep Carmen's agreement as a recommendation, not a completed account change. No competitor names, locations, price comparisons, booking claims, or any suggestion that this client joined an Accelerator. The copy follows this now; recheck it after any edits.
Whitney to confirm the carousel's ADS invitation, the email reply invitation, the following-week timing, the email segment and the 10:00 a.m. Central send time.
Check whether prior angle angle_b8c656564c3f3b524b723ae7 is an unpublished version of this idea. If the same central point was published in the last 90 days, hold this pack.
stronger_with_permission: Erin's own explanation of why the nearby venue made sense: some couples had told the team they couldn't afford the other venue but could afford theirs. It is kept out because the brief bars price comparisons.
The actual venue names and locations, which would make the different-market contrast concrete. They are kept out by the brief.
Whether Carmen's recommendation was implemented in the account and what happened afterward. The brief allows no implementation or results claim.
Carmen's line "Definitely not." agreeing with the exclusion. It is held back because it only reads clearly next to the venue name it answered.
change_notes: Added the third Reel (stance), as the pack requires. It states Whitney's view on the same central point and uses the review as proof in two lines, with no new facts.
The email now opens on the moment itself (Carmen, the search terms, another venue's name) and uses Carmen's and Erin's exact short lines in place of the abstract paraphrase.

The email lost formal filler ("relevant information for an expert to understand", "meaningful basis"). It now has one bold key line, a personal "Honestly?" beat and the Accelerator descriptor exactly as approved.
Rewrote the subject lines and preview so none collides with the carousel title or the Reel hooks. The preview now finishes the subject line's thought.

The story Reel is now spoken and casual, in her on-camera rhythm. Its stiff opener ("the client's team explained why a competing venue's name made sense there") is replaced with a concrete scene, and Whitney is never implied to be on the call.
Gave each Reel a specific cover and on-screen hook that names Google Ads, search terms or competing venues. Every cover and caption hook is distinct across the pack.
The b-roll screens now tell the turn in three plain lines (situation, what the team knew, the different-market recommendation), with no venue names.
Restructured every caption to Savannah's framework. Each one now opens on the reader's world (search terms, tours, inquiry calls) before the story, which the drafts skipped.
Cut the abstract stand-ins ("judgment", "meaningful place", "room", "contributions") and the closing kickers. Every piece keeps at most one contrast construction.
Rebuilt the carousel slides as short stacked lines of about 20 to 50 words, with at most one bold line each. Added a "We believe" slide and a final slide for both managed and guided readers.
Changed "before considering theirs" to "as well as theirs" or "too" throughout to match the brief's supporting details. Kept the exclusion as Carmen's agreement or recommendation everywhere.
Left out Erin's affordability line and her "way bigger than we are" remark, since both hint at the price comparison the brief keeps out. Both are listed under stronger_with_permission.
Varied the shared wording between siblings (Carmen's default, couples considering the nearby venue) so no 6-word span repeats across pieces. The quotes are split between pieces.
